ruling_text:
Case Number:
23PSCV00098
Hearing Date:

March 20, 2026
Dept:

G
Defendants  Luis Faura and Manuel G. Fernandez’s Motion for Summary Judgment, or in the  Alternative, Summary Adjudication
Respondent:  Plaintiff CMBG Advisors, Inc.

Plaintiff  CMBG Advisors, Inc.’s Motion for Summary Judgment
Respondent:  Defendants Luis Faura and Manuel G. Fernandez

TENTATIVE  RULING
Defendants  Luis Faura and Manuel G. Fernandez’s Motion for Summary Judgment, or in the  Alternative, Summary Adjudication is DENIED.
Plaintiff  CMBG Advisors, Inc.’s Motion for Summary Judgment is DENIED.

BACKGROUND
This  is an action for breach of fiduciary duty arising from the defendants’ roles as  corporate officers of a business.
C&F  Foods, Inc. (C&F) was the parent company of C&F Foods Logistics  Services, Inc. (C&F Logistics) and Arizona Flexible Packaging, Inc.  (Arizona Packaging), companies engaged in food packing and export.
Defendant Luis Faura (Faura) served as  C&F’s president, chief executive officer, and member of the board of  directors while defendant Manuel G. Fernandez (Fernandez) served as C&F’s  secretary and chairman of the board of directors.
Between 2013 and 2020, Faura and Fernandez  (collectively, Defendants) allegedly conducted numerous business transactions  to C&F’s detriment for their own personal benefit and for the benefit of separate  companies they created.
On January 15,  2020, on behalf of C&F, C&F Logistics, and Arizona Packaging  (collectively, Assignors), Faura made plaintiff CMBG Advisors, Inc. (CMBG) the  assignee for the benefit of Assignors’ creditors.
CMBG alleges Defendants also transferred  C&F’s assets to their other companies without CMBG’s consent.
On  January 11, 2023, CMBG filed the Complaint, alleging a single cause of action  for breach of fiduciary duty against Defendants.
On  November 8, 2024, Defendants filed a motion for summary judgment, or in the  alternative, summary adjudication.
On  November 13, 2024, CMBG filed a motion for summary judgment.
The  parties filed multiple separate statements with responses in support of the two  motions.
Defendants’ separate statement  with CMBG’s responses, filed on January 16, 2025, is referenced as the First  UMF, which spans numbers 1 to 89.
CMBG’s  separate statement with Defendants’ responses, filed on January 24, 2025, is  referenced as the Second UMF, which spans numbers 90 to 206.
CMBG’s separate statement with Defendants’  responses, filed on January 16, 2025, is referenced as Third UMF, which spans  numbers 1 to 121.
Defendants’ separate  statement without responses, filed on December 12, 2025, is referenced as  Fourth UMF, which spans numbers 90 to 111.
CMBG’s separate statement with Defendants’ responses, filed on December  23, 2025, filed on December 23, 2025, is referenced as Fifth UMF, which spans  numbers 1 to 53.
On  January 28, 2026 and February 6, 2026, the court considered the parties’ oral  arguments on the motions for summary judgment and continued the hearing for  additional briefing regarding Corporations Code §158.
Defendants filed their supplemental brief on  February 13, 2026, while Plaintiff filed its supplemental brief on February 19,  2026.
The court considered all of the  parties’ moving briefs, oppositions, replies, and supplemental briefing.
The court, however, did not consider Defendants’  “pocket brief” filed on March 12, 2026.
This  case is set for a mandatory settlement conference and a continued hearing on  the motions on March 20, 2026.

REQUESTS  FOR JUDICIAL NOTICE
CMBG  requests that the court take judicial notice of government and court records  and a statement for standards of accounting from the American Institute of  Certified Public Accountants.
The court  takes judicial notice of the requested documents under Evidence Code section  452, subdivisions (d) and (h).
Defendants  request that the court take judicial notice of grant deeds recorded in the Los  Angeles County Recorder’s Office.
The  court takes judicial notice of the requested documents under Evidence Code  section 452, subdivision (h).
CMBG  also requests that the court take judicial notice of the original articles of  incorporation of C&F, the certificate of amendment of the articles of  incorporation, the restated articles of incorporation, and a website listing  from the California Secretary of State.
The  court takes judicial notice of the requested documents under Evidence Code  section 452, subdivision (h).

EVIDENTIARY  OBJECTIONS
CMBG  objects to the Serota Declaration, Faura Declaration, Anglin Declaration, and  Amolyan Declaration.
All of these  objections are overruled.

ANALYSIS
Both  parties move for summary judgment on the sole cause of action for breach of  fiduciary duty.
For the following  reasons, the court

DENIES
the motions.

Legal  Standard
A  motion for summary judgment or adjudication provides “courts with a mechanism  to cut through the parties’ pleadings in order to determine whether, despite  their allegations, trial is in fact necessary to resolve their dispute.”
(
Aguilar v. Atlantic Richfield Co.
(2001) 25 Cal.4th 826, 843.)
It must be  granted “if all the evidence submitted, and ‘all inferences reasonably  deducible from the evidence’ and uncontradicted by other inferences or  evidence, show that there is no triable issue as to any material fact and that  the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.”'
(
Adler v. Manor Healthcare Corp.
(1992) 7 Cal.App.4th 1110, 1119, quoting Code Civ. Proc., § 437c, subd.  (c).)
To establish a triable issue of  material fact, the opposing party must produce substantial responsive evidence.
(
Sangster v. Paetkau
(1998) 68  Cal.App.4th 151, 166.)
Courts “liberally  construe the evidence in support of the party opposing summary judgment and  resolve doubts concerning the evidence in favor of that party.”'
(
Dore v. Arnold Worldwide, Inc.
(2006)  39 Cal.4th 384, 389.)' “A motion for summary adjudication shall be granted only  if it completely disposes of a cause of action, an affirmative defense, a claim  for damages, or an issue of duty.”
(Code  Civ. Proc., § 437c, subd. (f)(1).)
Discussion
“The  elements of a cause of action for breach of fiduciary duty are the existence of  a fiduciary relationship, breach of fiduciary duty, and damages.”
(
Oasis West Realty, LLC v. Goldman
(2011) 51 Cal.4th 811, 820.)
Existence  of a Fiduciary Relationship
Defendants  owed fiduciary duties to C&F, and C&F assigned to CMBG the right to  prosecute an action on its behalf.
“Directors  owe a duty of highest good faith to the corporation and its stockholders,” and  “[t]he same duty of good faith in dealings, with or on behalf of the  corporation, is demanded of officers of the corporation.”
(
Burt v. Irvine Co.
(1965) 237  Cal.App.2d 828, 850.)
Directors and  officers do not owe a fiduciary duty to a corporation’s creditors.
(
Berg & Berg Enterprises, LLC v. Boyle
(2009) 178 Cal.App.4th 1020, 1037.)
However, “A cause of action is transferable, that is, assignable, by its  owner if it arises out of a legal obligation or a violation of a property  right. . . .”
(
Amalgamated Transit  Union, Local 1756, AFL-CIO v. Super. Ct.
(2009) 46 Cal.4th 993, 1003.)
Here,  Defendants were officers and directors of C&F and as such owed fiduciary  duties to C&F.
(First UMF Nos. 10,  11, 19; Third UMF Nos. 8–11.)
Defendants  argue at length that they do not owe fiduciary duties to C&F’s creditors,  including CMBG.
(Def. MSJ Brief, pp.  13–17; Def. Reply, pp. 2–3; Def. Opp., pp. 5–7.)
However, CMBG’s suit is not based on their  role as creditors but as the assignee of C&F’s rights, including the “[causes]  of action that are legally assignable” and “the right of [CMBG] to prosecute  any action in the name of . . . Assignors.”
(Third UMF Nos. 4–6.)
Therefore, the  court finds CMBG may bring this action based on the fiduciary relationship  between Defendants and C&F.
Breach  of Fiduciary Duty
To  determine whether Defendants breached a fiduciary duty, the court first examines  whether they are shielded from liability under the business judgment rule.
If not, then the court examines whether Defendants’  business conduct violated their fiduciary duties.
Business  Judgment Rule
The  business judgment rule does not shield Defendants from liability because the  circumstances inherently raise an inference of conflict of interest.
Under the business judgment rule, codified in  Corporations Code section 309, “A person who performs the duties of a director  . . . shall have no liability based upon any alleged failure to discharge the  person’s obligations as a director.”
(Corp. Code, § 309, subd. (c).)
The business judgment rule establishes a presumption that directors’  decisions are based on sound business judgment, and it prohibits courts from  interfering in business decisions made by the directors in good faith and in  the absence of a conflict of interest.
(
Lauckhart  v. El Macero Homeowners Assn.
(2023) 92 Cal. App. 5th 889, 906;

Lee v.  Interinsurance Exchange
(1996) 50 Cal.App.4th 694, 715.)
Applying this presumption, a court will not  substitute its judgment for the board of director’s judgment if the latter’s  decision can be attributed to any rational business purpose.
(
Lauckhart
,
supra
, at 906.)
However, “[a]n exception to this presumption  exists in circumstances which inherently raise an inference of conflict of  interest.”
(
Lee
,
supra
, at  715.)
The  parties dispute whether Defendants had a conflict of interest in the  transactions between C&F and Defendants’ other businesses.
(Def. MSJ Brief, pp. 17–18; CMBG Opp., pp. 16–18;  CMBG MSJ Brief, p. 25.)
However, the standard  is not whether there was an actual conflict but whether the circumstances “
inherently  raise an inference
of conflict of interest.”
(
Lee
,
supra
, 50 Cal.App.4th at  715, emphasis added.)
The  circumstances of this case raise an inference of conflict of interest.
Defendants were simultaneously directors and  officers of C&F and members and managers of businesses that did business  with C&F.
(Third UMF Nos. 8–11, 19–20.)
Defendants take issue with the vagueness and  characterizations of the business transactions, but they do not dispute that  such transactions occurred.
(Third UMF  No. 20.)
Defendants are not entitled to  the presumption of sound business judgment under the business judgment rule  because they were involved on both sides of multiple business transactions,  which raise an inference of conflict of interest.
Therefore, the business judgment rule does  not insulate Defendants from liability.
Good  Faith and Fairness of Transactions
As  a preliminary matter, to determine the good faith and fairness of the  transactions, the court must determine whether this case falls under the  standards of Corporations Code section 158, which applies to close  corporations, or Corporations Code section 310, which applies to other  corporations.
Under Section 158, a  “close corporation” is defined as “a corporation . . . whose articles contain, .  . . a provision that all of the corporation’s issued shares of all classes  shall be held of record by not more than a specified number of persons, not  exceeding 35, and a statement, ‘This corporation is a close corporation.’”
(Corp. Code, § 158, subd. (a).)
The  court notes that C&F was incorporated in 1977, after Section 158 took  effect in 1975.
Therefore, the court must  determine whether C&F satisfied the requirements to be a close corporation  under Section 158.
(CMBG Supp. Brief, RJN,  Exh. 1, p. 1.)
First, C&F’s original  articles of incorporation do not provide that the shares be held by a specified  number of less than 35 people.
(
See
CMBG  Supp. Brief, RJN, Exh. 1, pp. 1–2.)
Additionally,  the original articles of incorporation fail to contain an explicit statement  that C&F is a close corporation.
(
See
CMBG Supp. Brief, RJN, Exh. 1, pp. 1–2.)
Finally, when C&F filed restated articles of incorporation in 2015,  language designating it a close corporation was omitted.
Defendants  argue the provisions of Section 158 are a “safe harbor” for corporations which  choose to include the statutory language indicating a close corporation.
Defendants also argue the court must look to  the corporation’s actual structure and operation to determine whether the  corporations acted as a close corporation. (
See
Defendants’ Supp. Brief,  p.2.)
The court, however, is not  persuaded by Defendants’ arguments.
In  rejecting Defendants’ argument, the court notes that none of the cited cases permit  a corporation to ignore the statutory requirements of Section 158.
Thus,  the court finds that C&F was not a close corporation under Section 158.
Therefore, the court’s analysis will focus on  the good faith and fairness of Defendants’ transactions under Corporations Code  section 310.
A  transaction between a corporation and a corporation in which one of its  directors has a material financial interest is valid if the material facts as  to the transaction and as to such director’s interest are fully disclosed to  the shareholders and such transaction is approved by the shareholders in good  faith, with the shares owned by the interested director not being entitled to  vote.
(Corp. Code, § 310, subd. (a)(1).)
In the absence of any allegation or proof to  the contrary, ratification by the stockholders of an action by the directors is  presumed to be within the scope of their power as business managers of the  corporation.
(
Buck v. Tuxedo Land Co.
(1930) 109 Cal. App. 453, 461.)
If the  director’s material financial interest is not fully disclosed before the  transaction, the person asserting the validity of the transaction sustains the  burden of proving that the transaction was just and reasonable as to the  corporation at the time it was authorized, approved or ratified.
(Corp. Code, § 310, subd. (a)(3).)
Transactions between corporations and  directors or controlling shareholders are subject to “rigorous scrutiny,” and  “the burden is on the director or stockholder not only to prove the good faith  of the transaction but also to show its inherent fairness from the viewpoint of  the corporation and those interested therein.”
(
Burt
,
supra
, 237 Cal.App.2d at 850–851.)
As  recognized above, Defendants were simultaneously directors and officers of  C&F and members and managers of businesses that did business with  C&F.
(Third UMF Nos. 8–11, 19–20.)
Defendants argue that they, as the sole  shareholders of C&F, approved every transaction.
(Def. MSJ Brief, p. 20; Def. Reply, p. 3; Def.  Opp., p. 11.)
However, the parties  dispute whether Defendants consented to all transactions prior to each business  dealing.
(First UMF Nos. 20, 30; Second  UMF Nos. 173, 181.)
Moreover, Defendants  continued conducting business on C&F’s behalf after CMBG’s assignment for  the benefit of creditors, without CMBG’s consent.
(Second UMF Nos. 90–93, 95.)
Therefore, the court finds there remains a  triable issue of fact surrounding the good faith and fairness of transactions  between C&F and other companies managed by Defendants.
Damages
The  court determines there is a triable issue of material fact relating to the  amount of damages.
“For the breach of an  obligation not arising from contract, the measure of damages . . . is the  amount which will compensate for all the detriment proximately caused thereby,  whether it could have been anticipated or not.”
(Civ. Code, § 3333.)
The  issue of damages is complicated significantly by the possibility that  Defendants operated C&F and the companies that transacted with C&F as a  single enterprise.
CMBG alleges that  Defendants concentrated liabilities in C&F and concentrated assets in the  other companies so that Defendants could retain the assets after C&F’s  insolvency.
(CMBG MSJ Brief, pp. 17–25; CMBG  Reply, pp. 5–10; CMBG Opp., pp. 16–18.)
Defendants  counter that the alleged assets of the other companies never belonged to  C&F and that the court should respect the separate corporate forms.
(Def. Reply, pp. 4–5; Def. Opp, pp. 8–9,  14–15.)
If C&F and the other companies  were a single enterprise, then the damages may include the value of assets owned  by the separate companies; if C&F and the other companies were not a single  enterprise, then the damages only amount to the assets previously owned by C&F  and wrongfully transferred.
It  is undisputed that Defendants were simultaneously directors and officers of  C&F and member and managers of other companies.
(Second UMF Nos. 103–104.)
Defendants, however, contest the business  relationship between C&F and the other companies and whether the companies  comingled their assets.
(Second UMF Nos.  105–106, 164–165, 167–169; Third UMF Nos. 21–22, 68.)
Whether Defendants operated C&F and the  other companies as a single enterprise is a question of fact, and the court  cannot determine the amount of damages until that factual question is  resolved.
Therefore,  the court finds a triable issue of material fact exists regarding the amount of  damages recoverable in this case.
Accordingly,  since there are triable issues of material fact on the issues of breach of  fiduciary duty and damages, the court

DENIES
both parties’ motions.

CONCLUSION
For  these reasons, the motions for summary judgment and summary adjudication are

DENIED
.

defendants: Luis Faura and Manuel G. Fernandez
